To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mercury (Hg) induces a concentration-dependent increase of intracellular calcium ([Ca2+] i) levels in Madin-Darby canine kidney ( MDCK) cells.

the nephrotoxic metal Hg2+ increases intracellular free Ca(2+) levels in renal tubular MDCK cells via releasing store calcium and that this Ca2(2+) signal is mediated by protein kinase C but not by phospholipase.

mercury (Hg(2+)) induced Ca(2+) increases in Madin Darbey canine kidney (MDKC) cells via releasing Ca(2+) store from endoplasmic recticulum and that Hg(2+) also caused cytotoxic effects at higher concentrations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of mercury-induced renal tubular cell injury.
the effect of Hg2+ on Ca2+ signaling in renal tubular cell and its possible role in Hg2+ cytotoxicity.
the mechanism by which Hg2+ induces Ca2+ signals and cell death.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Hg2+-induced Ca2+i increase is a consequence of a Ca2+ influx, which is independent of phospholipoase C and is regulated by protein kinase C.
Hg2+-induced [Ca]i increase is a mechanism of Hg2+-mediated cytotoxicity.
mercury-induced cytotoxicity is mediated by a protein kinase C-regulatory mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mercury induces a protein kinase C-regu-lated Ca2+ increase in renal tubular MDCK cells and this Ca2+ increase may be involved in mercury-induced cytotoxicity.
Hg2+-induced Ca2+-increase is mediated by protein kinase C and phospholipase D and that the Ca2+-increase may be a contributing factor to Hg2+-mediated cell damage in renal tubules.
Hg2+-induced cytotoxicity in MDCK cells is due to both Ca2+ -dependent and -independent mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Hg2+-induced [Ca(2+)](i) increase in MDCK cells was not due to phospholipase (PLC) activation, which is a common pathway of [Ca(2+) ](i) increase induced by many toxicants.
Hg2+-induced cytotoxicity is associated with Ca2+ release from endoplasmic Ca2+ stores.
Hg2+, a nephrotoxic agent, can induce a protein kinase C-mediated Ca2+ increase via releasing Ca2+ from endoplasmic stores in renal tubular MDCK cells.
